Boundary proximity is primarily determined by a query's neighbor distance ratio (NDR): the ratio of its k-th nearest neighbor distance to its (k+1)-th nearest neighbor distance within the index graph. In HNSW specifically (as implemented in FAISS and hnswlib), boundary-proximate queries are those whose entry-point traversal at the top layer lands in a node whose neighborhood was built under a different embedding geometry—detectable because the greedy graph walk terminates at a local minimum that disagrees with a brute-force exhaustive search, a discrepancy Malkov & Yashunin (2018) term shortcut degradation. To instrument this live without full brute-force reranking, you can maintain a lightweight shadow exact index over a reservoir sample (~1–5% of the corpus), comparing ANN results against exact kNN on that sample at query time; a rising disagreement rate on the shadow index is an early-warning signal for boundary region corruption before aggregate recall@k degrades measurably. Pinecone's internal engineering posts and Weaviate's HNSW tuning documentation both recommend monitoring ef search parameter sensitivity as a proxy: if increasing ef from 64 to 256 materially changes retrieved sets for a significant fraction of queries (>5%), the index graph has accumulated enough shortcut degradation to warrant partial reindexing of affected segments. The operationally underappreciated signal is query-side NDR drift itself: if your embedding model is being fine-tuned, the NDR distribution of the query population shifts, so a query that was boundary-distant last week can become boundary-proximate this week without any document corpus change—making static instrumentation thresholds unreliable.

Fallback to exact search offers the strongest consistency guarantee—recall@k = 1.0 by definition—but its latency scales as O(N·d) against corpus size, making it viable only for corpora under ~1M vectors or with aggressive pre-filtering that reduces the candidate set; Milvus's "growing segment" architecture exploits this by routing new/unstable vectors to a flat IVF index while the main HNSW index stabilizes, effectively partitioning exact-search cost to a small volatile subset. On-demand local reindexing—rebuilding the HNSW neighborhood graph for the ~M_ef nodes surrounding the detected boundary query—offers a durable fix with sub-second execution on small neighborhoods (~500 nodes, ~50ms in hnswlib), but introduces a write-read race condition: concurrent queries hitting the same neighborhood during reindexing either see the stale graph or must be held behind a lock, and neither option is acceptable in a sub-100ms RAG serving SLA without careful copy-on-write segment management. The pipeline-level caching interaction is the critical subtlety most implementations miss: if you cache ANN results by query embedding (as LangChain's caching layer and Redis-based semantic caches do), a successful remediation that returns corrected results for query Q will not propagate to cached near-duplicates of Q, leaving semantically similar queries continuing to retrieve stale neighborhoods until TTL expiry—you must invalidate by neighborhood ID rather than by query hash to achieve cache consistency under local reindexing. The practical resolution most production systems converge on is a tiered response: ef amplification first (latency-cheap, catches moderate degradation), exact search on the shadow reservoir as a consistency check (cheap because reservoir is small), and local reindexing deferred to an async queue that processes affected neighborhoods within one replication lag cycle—accepting that the current query pays degraded recall while future queries to the same region benefit from the repair.
